note: Backup content for the trader's corner and learn cards. Used in order whenever the AI writer is unavailable or its text fails a check. Education only: no item recommends a trade or predicts a price.

quiz.question: In the symbol XAU/USD, what does XAU stand for?
quiz.explanation: XAU is the international code for one troy ounce of gold. XAG is silver.

quiz.question: A troy ounce, the unit gold is quoted in, weighs about how much?
quiz.explanation: A troy ounce is about 31.1 grams, a little heavier than the everyday ounce of 28.35 grams.

quiz.question: What does CPI measure?
quiz.explanation: The Consumer Price Index tracks the price of a basket of goods and services, so it is a measure of inflation.

quiz.question: NFP is a monthly US report about what?
quiz.explanation: Non-Farm Payrolls counts jobs added or lost in the US economy, excluding farm work.

quiz.question: When is the US Non-Farm Payrolls report usually released?
options: The first Friday of the month
The last day of the month
quiz.explanation: It normally comes out on the first Friday of each month.

quiz.question: What is the FOMC?
options: The Federal Reserve committee that sets US interest rates
quiz.explanation: The Federal Open Market Committee decides US interest rate policy.

quiz.question: How many scheduled FOMC meetings are there in a normal year?
quiz.explanation: The committee has eight scheduled meetings a year, roughly every six weeks.

quiz.question: What is the 'spread' in trading?
options: The day's high minus its low
The gap between the buy and sell price
quiz.explanation: The spread is the difference between the ask (buy) price and the bid (sell) price.

quiz.question: What does leverage do?
options: Lets you control a larger position with less money
quiz.explanation: Leverage enlarges the position you control, which enlarges both gains and losses.

quiz.question: What is a stop-loss order for?
options: Closing a trade automatically to limit a loss
quiz.explanation: A stop-loss closes the position at a chosen price so a loss cannot keep growing.

quiz.question: What does the US Dollar Index (DXY) measure?
options: The dollar against a basket of major currencies
The price of gold in dollars
quiz.explanation: DXY compares the dollar with a basket of six major currencies, with the euro the largest part.

quiz.question: Gold pays no interest. Which of these is true?
options: Holding gold earns no interest or yield
Gold interest is set by the Fed
quiz.explanation: Gold has no yield, which is why interest rates matter so much to it.

quiz.question: What is a 'pip' in most currency pairs?
options: One whole unit of the currency
quiz.explanation: For most pairs a pip is 0.0001. Pairs with the Japanese yen use 0.01.

quiz.question: What does 'volatility' describe?
options: How much and how fast a price moves
quiz.explanation: High volatility means large, fast price swings; low volatility means a calm market.

quiz.question: Which two trading sessions overlap to create the busiest hours for gold?
quiz.explanation: The London and New York overlap usually has the most volume and the biggest moves.

quiz.question: What is 'slippage'?
options: An order filled at a different price than expected
quiz.explanation: In fast markets an order may be filled at a worse or better price than the one requested.

quiz.question: What does a 'hawkish' central bank lean toward?
options: Higher interest rates to fight inflation
quiz.explanation: Hawkish means favouring tighter policy and higher rates. Dovish is the opposite.

quiz.question: What is a 'margin call'?
options: A demand for more funds when losses shrink your margin
quiz.explanation: If losses reduce your account below the required margin, the broker asks for more funds or closes positions.

quiz.question: On a candlestick chart, what does the 'wick' show?
options: The highest and lowest price reached
quiz.explanation: The body shows the open and close; the wicks show the extremes reached in that period.

quiz.question: What does 'risk-to-reward ratio' compare?
options: What you could lose to what you could gain
quiz.explanation: It compares the planned loss if wrong with the planned gain if right.

quiz.question: PCE is the inflation measure most closely watched by whom?
quiz.explanation: The Federal Reserve's 2% inflation goal is defined using the PCE price index.

quiz.question: What is a 'demo account' used for?
quiz.explanation: A demo account lets you practise in live market conditions without risking real money.

quiz.question: Which metal has the symbol XAG?
quiz.explanation: XAG is silver. Ag comes from argentum, the Latin word for silver.

quiz.question: What does GDP measure?
options: The value of goods and services an economy produces
quiz.explanation: Gross Domestic Product is the total value of what an economy produces in a period.

rule.title: Risk a small part, never the account
rule.text: Many traders cap the risk on any single trade at 1 to 2 percent of the account. A run of losses then hurts, but it does not end the journey.

rule.title: Decide the exit before the entry
rule.text: Know where you are wrong before you open a trade. A stop-loss chosen calmly in advance is better than a decision made in panic.

rule.title: Respect the news calendar
rule.text: Prices can jump in seconds around CPI, NFP and Fed decisions. Check the calendar before you trade, not after.

rule.title: Leverage cuts both ways
rule.text: Leverage multiplies losses exactly as it multiplies gains. Smaller leverage gives a trade room to breathe.

rule.title: No trade is also a position
rule.text: Staying out of an unclear market is a decision, not a missed chance. Capital you keep is capital you can use later.

rule.title: Never add to a losing trade to feel better
rule.text: Averaging down without a plan turns a small mistake into a large one. If the reason for the trade is gone, the trade should be too.

rule.title: Keep a trading journal
rule.text: Write down why you entered, where you exited and how you felt. Patterns in your own behaviour are the most useful ones to find.

rule.title: Trade the plan, not the mood
rule.text: Fear and greed arrive after the trade is open. A written plan made beforehand is what protects you from them.

rule.title: One bad day should not need a great day
rule.text: Set a daily loss limit. When it is reached, stop. Chasing losses is how a bad day becomes a bad month.

rule.title: Size the position from the stop
rule.text: First decide where the stop goes, then choose a size so that distance equals the amount you are willing to lose.

rule.title: Spreads widen when it matters
rule.text: Around news and at the daily market close, spreads on gold can widen sharply. A stop placed too tight may be hit by the spread alone.

rule.title: Do not trade money you need
rule.text: Money for rent, fees or emergencies has no place in a trading account. Pressure makes every decision worse.

rule.title: Consistency beats size
rule.text: Small, repeatable results compound. One oversized trade can erase months of careful work.

rule.title: A win does not prove the method
rule.text: One good result can come from luck. Judge an approach over many trades, not one.

rule.title: Learn the product first
rule.text: Know the contract size, the value of one dollar of movement, the margin needed and the trading hours before placing a trade.

rule.title: Protect profit, do not just hope
rule.text: A plan should say what happens when a trade goes well too, such as moving the stop to break-even at a set point.

rule.title: Step away after a big loss
rule.text: The urge to win it back at once is strongest right after a loss, and it is when judgement is weakest.

rule.title: Weekend gaps are real
rule.text: Markets can reopen on Monday far from Friday's close. A stop-loss does not guarantee the price at which a weekend position closes.

rule.title: Demo first, real later
rule.text: Test a method on a demo account until the rules are clear. Real money adds emotion, not skill.

rule.title: Avoid trading when tired or upset
rule.text: Your state of mind is part of your risk. If you would not drive, do not trade.

rule.title: Check more than one timeframe
rule.text: A move that looks huge on a 5-minute chart may be nothing on the daily chart. Look at the bigger picture first.

rule.title: Be wary of anyone promising sure profits
rule.text: No signal, robot or mentor can promise returns. A promise of certain profit is the most reliable sign of a scam.

rule.title: Costs add up
rule.text: Spread, commission and overnight swap are paid on every trade. Frequent trading needs a bigger edge just to cover them.

rule.title: Review weekly, not after every trade
rule.text: Judging yourself trade by trade leads to constant changes. Review a week of trades together and adjust once.

fact.text: Gold's chemical symbol, Au, comes from the Latin word aurum, meaning shining dawn.
Gold is quoted in troy ounces. One troy ounce is about 31.1 grams, slightly heavier than a regular ounce.
Almost all the gold ever mined still exists in some form, because gold does not rust or corrode.
Central banks around the world hold tens of thousands of tonnes of gold as part of their reserves.
Until 1971 the US dollar could be converted into gold at a fixed rate of 35 dollars an ounce. That link was ended by President Nixon.
Pure gold is 24 karat. 22 karat gold is about 91.6 percent pure, and 18 karat is 75 percent.
Gold is so soft and malleable that a single ounce can be beaten into a sheet covering several square metres.
The London bullion market sets a benchmark gold price twice every business day, known as the LBMA Gold Price.
A standard 'Good Delivery' gold bar held by central banks weighs about 400 troy ounces, roughly 12.4 kilograms.
Spot gold trades almost around the clock from Monday to Friday, passing from Asia to London to New York.
India and China are the world's two largest consumer markets for gold jewellery.
Gold conducts electricity well and does not tarnish, which is why small amounts are used in phones and computers.
The gold-silver ratio tells you how many ounces of silver it takes to buy one ounce of gold. Traders watch it to compare the two metals.
The US dollar is involved in the large majority of all foreign exchange trades, more than any other currency.
The foreign exchange market is the largest financial market in the world, with trillions of dollars traded every day.
The United States holds the largest official gold reserve of any country, more than 8,000 tonnes.
Much of the US gold reserve is stored at Fort Knox in Kentucky.
Gold is priced in US dollars worldwide, so a change in the dollar's value affects what gold costs in every other currency.
The Federal Reserve aims for inflation of 2 percent a year over the longer run.
The first gold coins of a standard weight are believed to have been struck in the ancient kingdom of Lydia, in today's Turkey.
South Africa's Witwatersrand basin has produced a large share of all the gold ever mined.
A Fed 'dot plot' shows where each policymaker expects interest rates to be in the coming years. It is published four times a year.
The word 'carat' for gemstones and 'karat' for gold both trace back to the carob seed, once used as a small weight.
Gold melts at about 1,064 degrees Celsius.

myth.myth: Gold always goes up in a crisis.
myth.truth: Often, but not always. In a sudden rush for cash, investors sometimes sell gold too, and it can fall with everything else for a while.
Leverage only makes each move count for more. It enlarges losses by exactly the same amount as gains.

myth.myth: A stop-loss guarantees my exit price.
myth.truth: A normal stop becomes a market order when triggered. In a fast market or after a gap it can be filled at a worse price.

myth.myth: Good news for the US economy is always good for gold.
myth.truth: Strong US data can lift the dollar and interest-rate expectations, and both of those tend to weigh on gold.

myth.myth: You need a lot of money to learn trading.
myth.truth: Learning needs time and discipline, not capital. A demo account costs nothing and uses live prices.

myth.myth: Professional traders win most of their trades.
myth.truth: Many successful traders are wrong often. What matters is that losses are kept small relative to gains.

myth.myth: The more you trade, the more you make.
myth.truth: Every trade has a cost. Overtrading raises costs and usually lowers the quality of decisions.

myth.myth: Gold and the dollar always move in opposite directions.
myth.truth: They often do, since gold is priced in dollars, but there are periods when both rise or both fall together.

myth.myth: A trading robot removes the risk.
myth.truth: An automated system only follows rules. If the rules stop suiting the market, it loses money without hesitation.

myth.myth: Inflation going up means gold must go up.
myth.truth: What matters more is how interest rates respond. If rates rise faster than inflation, gold can struggle.

myth.myth: Paid signals are a shortcut to profit.
myth.truth: Nobody can know the next move for certain. Following signals without understanding them leaves you unable to manage the trade.

myth.myth: A market that has fallen a lot is bound to bounce.
myth.truth: Price has no memory of what is 'too low'. Falling markets can keep falling for longer than expected.

myth.myth: Forex trades 24 hours a day, 7 days a week.
myth.truth: It trades around the clock on weekdays only. It closes on Friday evening in New York and reopens on Sunday.
Charts show what price has done and where others may be watching. They describe probabilities, not certainties.
Position size should come from the planned risk, not from how sure you feel. Feeling certain is not evidence.

myth.myth: News trading is easy because the number is public.
myth.truth: Markets react to the difference from expectations, often within a second, and spreads widen sharply at that moment.

lesson.title: What is XAU/USD?
points: XAU is the code for one troy ounce of gold; USD is the US dollar.
The price shows how many dollars one ounce of gold costs.
It moves when demand for gold changes or when the dollar itself gets stronger or weaker.
lesson.takeaway: Gold's price is really a relationship between gold and the dollar.

lesson.title: Why interest rates matter to gold
points: Gold pays no interest, while bonds and savings do.
When rates are high, holding gold means giving up more income.
When rates fall, that cost shrinks and gold becomes more attractive to hold.
lesson.takeaway: Watch what the market expects from interest rates.

lesson.title: Why the dollar matters to gold
points: Gold is priced in US dollars everywhere.
A stronger dollar makes gold more expensive for buyers using other currencies.
A weaker dollar makes it cheaper for them, which can support demand.
lesson.takeaway: Dollar strength and gold often pull in opposite directions.

lesson.title: What is CPI?
points: The Consumer Price Index measures how prices of everyday goods and services change.
It is the best-known measure of inflation in the US.
Markets compare the released number with the forecast, and the surprise is what moves prices.
lesson.takeaway: It is the gap from expectations that matters, not the number alone.

lesson.title: What is Non-Farm Payrolls?
points: It reports how many jobs the US economy added or lost in a month.
It comes with the unemployment rate and average hourly earnings.
It is usually released on the first Friday of the month and often causes sharp moves.
lesson.takeaway: Jobs data shapes what the market expects from the Fed.

lesson.title: What does the Fed do?
points: The Federal Reserve is the central bank of the United States.
Its FOMC committee sets the target for short-term interest rates eight times a year.
Its two goals are stable prices and maximum employment.
lesson.takeaway: Fed decisions are among the biggest scheduled events for gold.

lesson.title: Bid, ask and spread
points: The bid is the price at which you can sell; the ask is the price at which you can buy.
The spread is the difference between them and is a cost on every trade.
Spreads widen when the market is thin or news is breaking.
lesson.takeaway: A trade starts slightly negative because of the spread.

lesson.title: What is leverage?
points: Leverage lets you control a position larger than your deposit.
With 1:100 leverage, 100 dollars controls 10,000 dollars of exposure.
A 1 percent move against you would then equal your whole deposit.
lesson.takeaway: Leverage is a tool for efficiency, and a common cause of blown accounts.

lesson.title: What is margin?
points: Margin is the deposit your broker holds while a leveraged trade is open.
Free margin is what is left to absorb losses or open new trades.
If losses use it up, the broker may close positions automatically.
lesson.takeaway: Keep plenty of free margin; never trade at the limit.

lesson.title: Position sizing in three steps
points: Decide how much money you accept losing on the trade.
Decide where the stop-loss goes and measure that distance.
Choose the size so that distance equals that amount of money.
lesson.takeaway: The stop sets the size, not the other way round.

lesson.title: Risk-to-reward ratio
points: It compares the planned loss with the planned gain.
Risking 10 dollars to aim for 20 is a ratio of 1 to 2.
With 1 to 2 you can be wrong more often than right and still not lose overall.
lesson.takeaway: You do not need to be right most of the time.

lesson.title: The three trading sessions
points: Asia opens the day and is usually the quietest for gold.
London brings a jump in volume.
New York overlaps with London for a few hours, usually the most active time.
lesson.takeaway: The time of day changes how a market behaves.

lesson.title: Reading a candlestick
points: Each candle shows four prices for a period: open, high, low and close.
The thick body runs from the open to the close.
The thin wicks show the highest and lowest prices reached.
lesson.takeaway: One candle is a small story of a period's trading.

lesson.title: Support and resistance
points: Support is an area where falling prices have paused or turned before.
Resistance is an area where rising prices have paused or turned before.
They are zones that many people watch, not exact lines.
lesson.takeaway: Levels show where attention is, not what must happen.

lesson.title: What is a pivot point?
points: A pivot is the average of the previous day's high, low and close.
Support and resistance levels are calculated above and below it.
They are plain arithmetic that many traders use as reference points.
lesson.takeaway: Pivot levels are a shared map, not a forecast.

lesson.title: Hawkish and dovish
points: A hawkish central bank leans toward higher rates to control inflation.
A dovish one leans toward lower rates to support growth.
Markets react to changes in tone as well as to actual decisions.
lesson.takeaway: Listen to the wording, not only the rate.

lesson.title: What is a trading plan?
points: It states what you trade, when, and how much you risk.
It defines the conditions for entering and for exiting.
It is written before trading, when you are calm.
lesson.takeaway: A plan turns decisions into rules you can review.

lesson.title: Why keep a journal?
points: Record the reason, the result and your state of mind for each trade.
Review it weekly to find repeated mistakes.
It shows your real behaviour, which memory tends to flatter.
lesson.takeaway: You cannot fix what you do not record.

lesson.title: What are bond yields?
points: A yield is the return an investor earns for holding a bond.
The US 10-year yield is a key reference for the whole market.
Rising yields make interest-paying assets more attractive compared with gold.
lesson.takeaway: Yields and gold frequently move in opposite directions.

lesson.title: What is a safe haven?
points: A safe haven is an asset investors turn to in uncertain times.
Gold, the US dollar and government bonds are common examples.
The label describes a tendency, not a guarantee.
lesson.takeaway: Safe havens can still fall.
